transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-24
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (CTO, Starlight), Kyla Wong (Lead ML Engineer), Omar Hassan (Infra), Leah Park (PM)

Summary (auto): Discussed integration options for Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Focus on SDK support (Python/JS), LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, routing through customer's gateway, per-route quotas, and observability integration (OpenTelemetry, tracing, cost hooks). Agreed on follow-ups: share example repos, security docs, and run a small benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time today. quick intro, i'm jordan, i'm the account lead on this. priya is our solutions engineer — she'll dig into the integration details. alex is on for any infra questions. how are you all?
[00:08] Mark: hey jordan, thanks. good — busy quarter but excited to chat. i'll give a quick overview of why we're evaluating redwood.
[00:15] Mark: so starlight has been prototyping assistant features for our field tools. we've used a mix of hosted APIs and some self-hosted models but performance and cost variability have been an issue, so we're exploring a platform that lets us start hosted and then move to dedicated capacity or private if needed.
[00:35] Jordan: totally makes sense, that's a pattern we see a lot. priya — want to walk through how you'd integrate from the sdk/llm client side?
[00:42] Priya: yeah for sure. at a high level we have official python and js sdks. python's main client maps cleanly to langchain: you can swap in the RedwoodLLM class, and we also provide an adapter for LlamaIndex. i can show a snippet but basically it's plug-and-play for common chains.
[01:05] Kyla: quick q — do you support streaming responses in the langchain connector? we rely on streaming for our UI so partial tokens are important.
[01:12] Priya: yes — streaming is supported by our python sdk and the langchain wrapper surfaces the token stream as the usual async iterator. there can be small timing differences depending on hosted vs dedicated because of batching. small caveat: when you're on dedicated with aggressive batching you might see slightly higher initial latency but better throughput per-dollar.
[01:34] Omar: on the infra side, we have an internal gateway/proxy that routes all outbound to external APIS through our edge. how does that work with redwood's hosted api — do you allow static IPs or will we need to open wide egress?
[01:47] Alex: good question. hosted customers typically use our standard endpoints; we publish a set of IP ranges for allowlisting. for stricter setups we recommend either dedicated endpoints with VPC egress or our private (VPC) deployment. dedicated can provide fixed egress via customer VPC peering and NAT — that tends to fit teams that require strict egress controls.
[02:08] Omar: ok that helps. do you offer a gateway/proxy-friendly auth flow? we prefer not to leak tokens in client side code.
[02:15] Priya: yes — we often recommend an internal token proxy that mints short-lived tokens for clients. Redwood supports API keys, and for private/dedicated you can integrate with your KMS and SSO for service-to-service tokens. we also support JWTs via our gateway so the token doesn't need to be baked into end-user bundles.
[02:32] Leah: curious about rate limits — can we do per-route or per-team quotas? our usage varies a lot between teams.
[02:39] Jordan: yep we have quota primitives. hosted offering has per-api-key quotas and rate limits with soft and hard thresholds. dedicated adds more granularity — route based policies, per-team rate buckets, and custom throttling rules. you can also set circuit-breaker style fallbacks to a cheaper/smaller model if thresholds are hit.
[02:58] Kyla: and are those limits enforced at the edge or at your runtime? we need enforcement upstream to avoid bursts hitting our infra.
[03:05] Priya: enforcement is at our gateway layer and runtime; when you're in dedicated or private, you can push those policies into your control plane. additionally, Redwood has SDK hooks to expose token consumption so your frontend can display backpressure/usage signals.
[03:19] Mark: about observability — we have an existing stack: prometheus + grafana, jaeger, and internal cost dashboards. how does Redwood tie in?
[03:28] Alex: we export metrics for per-route latency, token counts, error rates; metrics can be pushed via our metrics forwarder to prometheus or you can consume them via our observability API. for tracing, we have OpenTelemetry spans emitted from runtime; in private deployments those spans can be sent directly to your jaeger/OTLP collector.
[03:44] Kyla: would we get token-level cost breakdowns? we need to attribute costs to teams and features.
[03:50] Jordan: yes, our console provides token-level billing by api-key/route and we can stream usage events to a webhook so you can ingest them into your cost dashboard. with dedicated we can also provide hourly/route-level granularity in the CSV exports.
[04:05] Kyla: nice. for model adapters — we use LlamaIndex heavily. is the adapter maintained upstream or do we need to fork?
[04:13] Priya: we maintain an official LlamaIndex adapter and a LangChain connector. they're in our examples repo; we keep them updated for major breaking changes but if you have custom prompt managers you might extend them locally. i'll share the repo after the call.
[04:27] Kyla: any gotchas about tokenization differences or stop-token handling? we've seen mismatch issues when switching model backends.
[04:34] Priya: good point — tokenization can differ between model families. our runtime normalizes token counting for billing, but prompts may need small tweaks for stop tokens. we recommend a short eval pass where we run a representative set of prompts through the candidate model and compare outputs; we'll help with the tooling for that.
[04:51] Mark: on security/compliance: SOC 2 is a must, and the legal team will want to see data retention and audit logs. do you have those?
[04:59] Jordan: yes — we have SOC 2 Type II, and we provide audit logs and configurable retention windows. for private deployments we offer customer-managed keys and no-retention options. i'll attach our security pack and the SOC2 report in the follow-up.
[05:12] Leah: do you do per-request PII scrubbing or is that on our side?
[05:17] Priya: we offer optional in-flight scrubbing rules at the gateway level, though most customers implement pre-processing in their app. we can show a sample middleware pattern for that.
[05:26] Omar: about benchmarks — we want to test latency at our 90th percentile with a 512-token context and about 50 QPS. can you run a small benchmark on hosted and estimate dedicated sizing?
[05:36] Alex: absolutely. if you send the traffic profile (token lengths, qps distribution) and the model family you prefer, we can run a benchmark and produce latency/throughput curves and recommended GPU counts for dedicated. typically for 50 QPS with 512 tokens, dedicated pools using A100-style instances get good latency; but pricing and model quantization will affect it.
[05:56] Kyla: we also hope to use quantized models for cost savings — does Redwood support int8/int4 quantized serving?
[06:03] Priya: yes, our runtime supports quantized execution paths and we have quantization profiles per model. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization levels based on workload and quality thresholds. we can include recommended profiles in the benchmark output.
[06:16] Mark: timeline — we're targeting a pilot in 6 weeks and production rollout in Q4. is that feasible?
[06:22] Jordan: pilot in 6 weeks is feasible. typical path: quick PoC (2-4 weeks) using hosted with some route rules, then pilot on Dedicated if performance/cost justify it. for private deployments timing varies based on infra approvals, but we can parallelize security review.
[06:36] Leah: pricing — can you ballpark hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity? we need ranges for the exec team.
[06:42] Jordan: i'll send tiered ballparks after the call — hosted per-token depends on model family (open vs finetuned) and throughput; dedicated is a commit with monthly charges — we give per-token effective costs lower than hosted at scale. i'll include examples in the follow-up.
[06:58] Kyla: curious about SDK versioning and breaking changes. we run automated integration tests; if you do a breaking change, what's the deprecation timeline?
[07:06] Priya: we follow semantic versioning for SDKs and maintain a changelog. breaking changes get announced with a deprecation window (usually 8-12 weeks) and we keep old minor versions supported for a period. we can add you to our early-deprecation list so you get heads-up emails.
[07:22] Mark: any limitations on files / multimodal requests? we do some embeddings for document search and occasional multimodal inference.
[07:30] Alex: embeddings are supported; for document search we provide bulk embed endpoints and async batch jobs. multimodal support varies by model — we can map your use-case to the right model. if you need on-prem multimodal, private deployment is usually the path.
[07:45] Leah: ok great. anything else from the redwood team?
[07:49] Jordan: just to recap next deliverables: priya will share example repo + langchain/llamaindex snippets; alex will outline benchmark plan and what data you should send; i'll send pricing ranges and security pack. we'll aim to get those out in 48-72 hours.
[08:05] Mark: perfect thanks. we'll assemble the sample prompts and QPS profile and send by friday.
[08:10] Kyla: one last operational q — does redwood support per-request metadata or tags that flow through traces so we can attribute to features?
[08:18] Priya: yes we have a metadata header you can pass (x-redwood-meta) that gets attached to billing/trace events; you can use it to tag team/feature ids. we'll include the header spec in the repo.
[08:29] Omar: and for long-running streaming connections, do you support reconnect semantics? we've had issues with connection churn.
[08:36] Alex: yes we recommend a resume token pattern for streams; our SDKs include helpers that automatically retry with backoff and resume partial streams where supported by the model. we'll show code samples.
[08:48] Jordan: ok great — if no further questions we'll wrap and follow up with the artifacts. thanks everyone.
[08:55] Mark: thanks all, appreciate it.

End of call.
